Exact recovery results concern the anchor rules; myopic temperature changes and risk-sensitive policies are controlled deformations of those rules. unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: With the notation of Section \ref{ptnb:sec:background}, we build a finite-horizon two-player game \parencite{OsborneRubinstein1994} played \emph{backward} from the output: a state records a position in the backward traversal (layer, neuron, plus game-specific bookkeeping for player turn and stream sign), and at each non-terminal state the active player either stops, moving to an absorbing cemetery state $\dagger$, or continues. Skip connections become random transitions to summand states; max-pooling sends players greedily to maximal-payoff states. Section \ref{ptnb:app:notation} collects the bookkeeping labels (Table \ref{ptnb:tab:notation}). The \ac{sg} value $V_p(s)$ is the $\gamma$-discounted expected payoff difference $r_p - r_{p'}$ of player $p$ and opponent $p'$ along trajectories from $s$ under the policies, expressed for the player $p$ in turn at $s$ by the Bellman recursion \begin{align}\label{ptnb:eq:bellman} V_p(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_x(s)} \Big\{ &r_p(s,a) - r_{p'}(s,a) \nonumber\\ &+ \gamma(s) \textstyle\sum_{s'} \P_x(s' \mid s,a)\, V_p(s') \Big\}, \end{align} whereas the \acl{rg} replaces the hard maximization at routing states by an entropy-regularized maximization over mixed routing decisions, whose value is the soft game value \eqref{ptnb:eq:soft-bellman}. Any player policies induce a backward trajectory measure $\Pi_x$ on trajectories $\zeta=(\zeta_0, \zeta_1, \dots)$ with a game-specific cumulative discount $d_t(\zeta)$ up to time $t$. The \textbf{discounted occupation measure} \parencite{Puterman1994mdp} \begin{align}\label{ptnb:eq:attribution} \Gamma_x(v) \coloneqq \E_{\zeta \sim \Pi_x}\!\left[ \textstyle\sum_t d_t(\zeta)\,\1\{\zeta_t = v\} \right] \end{align} quantifies how much weight the trajectories going through a state have.

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: The construction retains the full input dependence of Queries, Keys, Values, softmax, and LayerNorm statistics. It gives a mathematical DC representation of the forward map. Its existence does not establish numerical stability of the stream evaluation or attribution quality. The reciprocal-square-root pair already adds a common term with coefficient $M=(2\varepsilon^{3/2})^{-1}$, which grows rapidly as $\varepsilon$ decreases. Repeated products and squares can further amplify this common mass, so the recovered output may require cancellation between extremely large streams. The real-arithmetic proof supplies no floating-point error bound or practical runtime guarantee. Appendix \ref{app:transformer_dc_numeric} records a numerical diagnostic using a post-normalization block assembled from the same primitive pairs; its LayerNorm placement differs from Definition \ref{def:prenorm_transformer}. The attribution experiments in this thesis use the conditioned routing and attribution rules described in the following sections; they do not evaluate this new convex Transformer construction.

Equivariant Reynolds averaging optionally suppresses tokenization-grid artifacts \parencite{Wrobel2024} (\ac{rg}+Eq). Full KL formulation, oracle embedding, occupation-measure theorem and implementation are in Section \ref{ptnb:app:attention-subgame}. \label{ptnb:app:vit-extension}\label{sec:attention_routing_game}\label{ptnb:app:attention-subgame}

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: We first state the rule that the Routing-Game state-space construction below is designed to recover. We focus on a single attention head; the multi-head extension carries an additional head index $h$ and the recovery is per-head. Note that ViT-B/16 implements the Value projection as a single $D \times D$ linear $v = X W_v$ followed by a reshape into $n_h$ heads (the per-head matrix $W_v^{(h)} \in \RR^{D \times d_h}$ is the head-$h$ column block of the full $W_v$), so one input embedding $X_{k,e}$ feeds Value entries of every head and the per-head $R^X$ contributions sum at $X_{k,e}$ to give the total. The per-head description below applies unchanged. We omit the $\varepsilon$ stabilizer inside the attention block --- the surrounding ReLU recursion of \S\ref{ptnb:app:routing-attribution} carries its own $\varepsilon$ on every linear-routing state and that mechanism transfers to the $Av{+}W_v$ composite without modification, but tracking it through the tensor indexing here only obscures the structure.

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: The three methods share one pipeline: a stabilized split forward pass caching the original activations, a stabilized backward pass --- relevance-based for SplitLRP (initialized at the class-specific $\act{L}{+}$ and propagated by the $\varepsilon$-rule), sensitivity-based otherwise (the shifted recursions of \eqref{eq:shift_definition}) --- and a method-specific readout, with the resulting map bilinearly upsampled to the input resolution. The network can be split once per model. In the reported implementation, SplitCAM and SplitGrad take substantially longer per image than ordinary Grad-CAM and LayerCAM. Their timings are of the same order as the row labeled Guided Grad-CAM, but the released VGG-16 configuration dispatches Guided LayerCAM, limiting identification of that baseline. Section \ref{app:p1_timing} details this ambiguity and the measurement scope.

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: The split-based methods above read a fixed \ac{dc} decomposition. The complementary route of Chapter \ref{ch:game_theory} attributes through the equilibrium trajectory distribution of the \ac{sg} and \ac{rg}: the per-neuron difference of the two players' discounted occupation measures is the attribution map, and at the anchor temperature $\tau = 1$ this difference recovers the $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} family exactly (Theorem \ref{thm:lrp_recovery}), just as the plain gradient arises as a difference of occupation measures. Those equivalences --- the stopping and routing games, the recovery of gradients and of the $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} rule --- are \emph{defined and proven} in Chapter \ref{ch:game_theory} and are not restated here. This section collects only what turns those equilibria into concrete, tunable attribution maps: the \emph{modes} that deform the games, and the input-side \emph{technicalities} that raise attribution quality.

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: The split campaign evaluates pretrained VGG-16 and ResNet-18 on a custom 50-class ImageNet-S subset at $224\times224$ resolution. The source paper reports a 50-image validation split (one image per class) for selecting layer--formula combinations and a 566-image test split. Its released loader selects from the image--mask pairs available locally without the label-agreement filter used by the game campaign below; the historical sample membership cannot be recovered from these counts alone. The explanations target the model's predicted class, including for misclassified images, while localization is measured against the annotated object mask. For each method, localization-selected and Pixel-Flipping-selected configurations are retained. Full settings and results are given in Appendix \ref{app:saliency}.

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: Figure \ref{fig:vgg_saliency_comparison_main} qualitatively compares saliency maps from our split methods with their baseline counterparts at the best-performing layers. Mid-layer SplitCAM shares key visual characteristics with classical $\gamma$-\ac{lrp} from earlier layers. Compared to standard LayerCAM on the same layer it focuses more weight to all object pixels, while still marking the key object features as especially important. For $\alpha \ll 0.5$, SplitGrad yields less focused yet finely aligned gradients that closely follow image details. We attribute this to the Maxout activation retaining pre-activation information, unlike ReLU, which discards it in inactive neurons. Overall, mid-layer SplitCAM offers an effective balance between interpretability and focus (low entropy). Further qualitative examples are collected in Appendix \ref{app:saliency}.

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: Table \ref{tab:alpha_ablation_main} presents the performance of two selected SplitGrad and SplitCAM configurations across different shifting parameters $\alpha$, evaluated on the custom ImageNet-S test split. As introduced in Section \ref{sec:stabilization_dc}, the $\alpha$ value determines how strongly the backward pass is stabilized: $\alpha = 0$ results in no stabilization, and $\alpha = 0.5$ results in local sensitivities resembling scaled versions of the original network gradient. Within this ablation, reducing $\alpha$ from $0.5$ to $0.4$ improves Pointing Game and Attribution Localization for both configurations, while SplitCAM's PF$^{\mathrm{drop}}_{20}$ decreases from $1.607$ to $1.585$. SplitGrad reaches its highest PF$^{\mathrm{drop}}_{20}$ at $\alpha = 0.4$ and its highest localization scores at $\alpha = 0.35$; SplitCAM's Pointing Game and Attribution Localization optima occur at $0.4$ and $0.35$, respectively. Maximum Sensitivity is lowest at $\alpha = 0$ for both configurations. The sweep therefore supports a metric-dependent choice of $\alpha$ and does not isolate the effect of numerical stabilization from the change in attribution rule. The full $\alpha$ grid, including the comparison between the convex and the winner-takes-it-all max-pooling modes, is reported in Appendix \ref{app:ablation} (Table \ref{tab:alpha_comparison_by_method}).

unmatched_paragraphs.old_payload: When the cemetery absorbs a large fraction of trajectory mass, the total Hellinger distance mixes two effects: disagreement about \emph{whether} a trajectory survives and disagreement about \emph{where surviving trajectories go}. To isolate the second effect, we condition each model's trajectory law on the event that the trajectory reaches an ordinary input-layer state. The resulting scalar compares the two \emph{surviving} trajectory distributions directly and removes the common cemetery floor.
